title: Diagnose a crash using only logs and print statements
mechanism_check: Confirm the crash is real and repeatable: what exact input or action triggers it, every time.
Read the top of the stack trace or the last log lines before the crash — the final frame is usually the proximate cause, not the root.
Check whether it happens on other machines and users: one machine means environment, everyone means code.
improvised_tools: Print statements and log lines as the debugger — stderr beats stdout because it is unbuffered.
A second terminal tailing the log file live while you reproduce.
Timestamps on every log line to separate slow from stuck.
steps: Reproduce the crash three times and write down the exact trigger before touching code.
Add prints at function entries and exits along the suspected path, narrowing by halves.
Run once more and find the last print that fired — the fault sits between it and the next one.
Read that code slowly and state the mechanism aloud: what value could be null, empty, or out of range here.
Fix, remove the prints, re-run the repro to confirm.
stop_conditions: Stop if the crash moves or changes shape each run — that is a race or memory corruption, escalate to heavier tooling.
Stop if it only happens on hardware you cannot access — file it with the repro, do not guess.
Never ship a fix you cannot reproduce the bug for — no repro, no claim.

title: Build a minimal reproduction for any bug
mechanism_check: State the bug in one sentence: given this input, the system does X instead of Y.
Identify what the repro must exclude: network, database, other services, time-of-day.
Decide the pass-fail signal: what single output line or exit code proves the bug.
improvised_tools: A scratch directory and a single script file — not the full app.
A tiny script or direct call instead of the UI.
Hard-coded fixtures instead of the real database.
steps: Copy the failing flow into a standalone script with the smallest input that triggers it.
Delete setup code until the bug stops reproducing — the last deleted piece was necessary.
Keep deleting until removing anything kills the repro: what remains is minimal.
Run it twice to confirm it reproduces reliably, then attach it to the bug report.
Now fix against the repro, not the app.
stop_conditions: Stop shrinking if the bug needs the full environment — label it an integration bug and move to applied tooling.
Stop if the minimal repro contradicts your theory of the bug — believe the repro, restart diagnosis.
Do not file a bug report without a repro attached when one is physically possible.

title: Bisect a regression with no CI available
mechanism_check: Confirm it is a regression: the same action worked before and fails now — pin the last-known-good date.
Get the repro from entry developer-002: bisection needs a yes-or-no signal per commit.
Identify the commit range: last good to first bad, from memory, tags, or release notes.
improvised_tools: Git bisect as the machine, your repro script as the oracle.
A shell one-liner that runs the repro and echoes pass or fail per commit.
A stash or worktree so bisection never touches your working changes.
steps: Verify the repro passes on the old commit and fails on the new before starting.
Run git bisect start, mark bad on new, good on old.
At each bisect commit, run the repro and answer good or bad honestly.
When bisect lands on the culprit, read that diff alone — the regression is in it.
Write the fix against that diff, then re-run the full repro suite.
stop_conditions: Stop if the range is over fifty commits and each test takes minutes — narrow the range by release tags first.
Stop if good and bad flip inconsistently — the repro is flaky, fix the repro first (entry developer-010).
Never skip commits by hand during a bisect — the log of it is the evidence.

title: Recover from a bad deploy with a one-command rollback
mechanism_check: Confirm the deploy caused it: errors started within minutes of the deploy timestamp.
Decide rollback versus roll-forward: unknown cause or under fifteen minutes to roll back means roll back.
Know your rollback primitive before the incident: redeploy the old image, flip traffic, or revert the merge.
improvised_tools: The previous artifact or image tag as the lifeboat — keep N-1 deployable always.
One documented command, not a wiki page, to trigger the rollback.
The deploy timestamp in the incident timeline as the causality anchor.
steps: Declare the rollback out loud so the team stops parallel-debugging the new code.
Run the single rollback command against the N-1 artifact.
Verify the error rate returns to baseline in the dashboards before declaring done.
Freeze further deploys until the bad change is understood.
Schedule the postmortem while the timeline is fresh.
stop_conditions: Stop and roll forward instead if the bad deploy included a schema migration the old code cannot read.
Stop if the rollback itself errors — declare a wider incident and page the platform owner.
Never debug the new code on production traffic while users are down — restore service first.

title: Hotfix production from a read-only shell
mechanism_check: Confirm the fix location: the repro from developer-002 must point at one file or one config value.
Confirm the shell is truly read-only: no writes to disk, no package installs — config-only or env-var-only changes.
Assess blast radius: who is affected right now versus who the hotfix would touch.
improvised_tools: Environment variables and feature-flag toggles as the hotfix surface — no code changes from this shell.
Log tailing and metric queries as your eyes.
A second person on the call as the sanity check before you touch anything.
steps: State the exact change and its revert plan before executing anything.
Make the smallest possible change: toggle, threshold, or connection string — never logic.
Apply it, then watch the error rate for five full minutes.
If it works, open the real code fix immediately — a hotfix is a bandage with an expiry date.
Write the postmortem line: why the shell was the only option, and how to avoid it next time.
stop_conditions: Stop if the fix requires editing code on the box — that is not a hotfix, that is an uncontrolled deploy.
Stop if you cannot revert the change in under a minute — do not apply one-way doors from a shell.
Escalate to incident command (entry developer-036) if the first change does not move the metric.

title: Trace a request end to end with curl and timestamps
mechanism_check: Map the path first on paper: client to edge to service to database — what are the hops.
Confirm each hop logs something correlatable: request id, timestamp, or trace header.
Identify the slow or failing hop before tracing: which boundary does the symptom sit behind.
improvised_tools: Curl with timing flags as the synthetic client.
A unique request id you inject per trace so logs stay joinable.
Timestamp diffs between hop logs as the poor-man's trace waterfall.
steps: Generate one request with a unique id you control and record its start time.
Curl each hop directly where possible, noting status code and timing per hop.
Pull logs for that request id at each hop and line the timestamps up.
The hop with the gap or the error owns the bug — hand it over with the evidence.
Save the curl commands into the runbook (entry developer-020) so the next trace is faster.
stop_conditions: Stop if a hop will not accept your injected id — note the blind spot and escalate to the hop owner.
Stop if the request path crosses a system you have no read access to — request access, do not guess.
Never trace with production credentials from a personal machine.

title: Profile a slow endpoint with only logs and sampling
mechanism_check: Confirm it is slow, not down: p99 latency versus the SLO, and since when.
Separate code slowness from dependency slowness: which part of the trace dominates.
Check whether slowness correlates with load, time, or specific inputs.
improvised_tools: Millisecond timestamps bracketing suspect code blocks as manual spans.
Log sampling — every Nth request — so profiling does not become the bottleneck.
A load of one: replay a single slow request repeatedly for stable measurements.
steps: Pick the single slowest endpoint and one representative slow request.
Add timestamp brackets around the top-level phases: auth, query, serialize, render.
Run the request ten times and average each phase — the dominant phase wins.
Drill one level deeper inside the dominant phase and repeat.
Optimize only the proven dominant phase, then re-measure before touching anything else.
stop_conditions: Stop if phases all look equal and small — the slowness is queuing or GC, not code.
Stop if your instrumentation changes the timing — sample less, bracket wider.
Never optimize without a before measurement — no baseline, no claim of improvement.

title: Fix a broken build when the lockfile drifts
mechanism_check: Read the actual error first: dependency resolution failures name the conflicting package.
Determine the drift source: lockfile edited by hand, a range that floated, or a platform change.
Check whether main is broken for everyone or just you — one machine means your cache.
improvised_tools: A clean checkout in a temp directory as the ground truth.
The lockfile diff against main as the suspect list.
The package manager's own lock and verify command instead of guesswork.
steps: Reproduce the break in a clean checkout to rule out your local cache.
Read the lockfile diff: which entries changed, and which dependency pulled them.
Pin or regenerate the lockfile with the project's blessed command, never by hand-editing versions.
Run the full build once from clean to confirm green.
Commit the lockfile with a message naming the drifted package.
stop_conditions: Stop if the break comes from a yanked or compromised package — escalate to security, do not just pin around it.
Stop if regenerating changes hundreds of lines — something else moved, find it first.
Never commit a lockfile you have not built from clean.

title: Ship behind a feature flag when the release train is frozen
mechanism_check: Confirm the freeze rules: what is allowed — flags off by default usually are.
Confirm the flag defaults to OFF in every environment including production.
Identify the flag's kill path: who can flip it and how fast.
improvised_tools: A boolean flag plus an allowlist as the release vehicle.
The flag-off code path as your guaranteed safe default.
Dark-launch metrics that prove the new path works for one percent before one hundred.
steps: Wrap the new behavior so the flag-off path is byte-identical to current production.
Ship with the flag off and verify zero behavior change in production.
Enable for internal users first, watch errors for a full business cycle.
Ramp in stages with a written rollback line: flag off returns to old behavior in seconds.
Remove the flag within one quarter — flags are technical debt with interest.
stop_conditions: Stop if the flag cannot fully disable the new path — partial flags are not safe under a freeze.
Stop if the flag system itself is down — no flag, no ship.
Never leave a flag in permanently; schedule its removal at creation.

title: Quarantine a flaky test instead of deleting it
mechanism_check: Confirm flakiness, not a real failure: does it pass on retry with no code change.
Gather the rate: how often, and does it cluster by time, machine, or parallel load.
Capture the failure output three times — flaky tests usually show one of two signatures.
improvised_tools: A quarantine suite or tag as the holding pen — still runs, does not block merges.
Retry-with-logging to harvest failure signatures automatically.
The test's own history — the last twenty runs — as the flakiness evidence.
steps: Document the flake: rate, signatures, suspected cause, date quarantined.
Move the test to the quarantine suite so it runs but cannot block anyone.
Add the suspected cause as a comment and a ticket linking both.
Fix the root cause — timing, shared state, ordering — in the real code or test.
Promote it back only after fifty consecutive green quarantine runs.
stop_conditions: Stop if the test never fails in quarantine — the flake was environmental, investigate the environment.
Never delete a test for flakiness — quarantine preserves the signal.
Never let quarantine grow past ten percent of the suite — a full pen means a systemic problem.

title: Diagnose a memory leak from process metrics
mechanism_check: Confirm the leak shape: memory climbs monotonically and never returns after load drops.
Separate leak from cache: does usage fall when idle or only grow.
Check whether restarts reset it cleanly — a true leak returns on the same curve.
improvised_tools: Process RSS over time — one metric, one graph — as the leak detector.
Heap snapshots or allocation counters if the runtime exposes them — no profiler needed to start.
Request count alongside memory to separate per-request leaks from background leaks.
steps: Graph memory against time and against request count for one full cycle.
If memory tracks requests, the leak is in the request path — bisect by endpoint.
If it tracks time, the leak is background: timers, caches, listeners.
Halve the suspect code by disabling features until the curve flattens.
Fix, then run the same cycle and compare curves before declaring victory.
stop_conditions: Stop if the growth is sawtooth — climbs then drops — that is GC pressure, not a leak.
Stop if the process is third-party and you cannot change its code — mitigate with restarts and escalate.
Never fix a leak by raising the memory limit — that buys time, not a fix.

title: Tame an N+1 query found in production traffic
mechanism_check: Confirm the N+1 signature: query count grows linearly with items on the page or in the batch.
Find it in slow-query or ORM logs: repeated identical queries differing only in the id.
Measure the cost: queries per request times requests per second.
improvised_tools: The ORM's eager-loading or batch-loading option as the standard fix.
A query counter in tests that fails when queries exceed a budget.
The slow-query log as the production witness.
steps: Reproduce the page or batch locally with query logging on and count the queries.
Identify the loop: which association is fetched per item instead of once.
Switch to eager or batched loading for that association.
Re-run and confirm the query count is flat regardless of item count.
Add a query-count assertion so the N+1 cannot silently return.
stop_conditions: Stop if eager loading explodes memory — paginate or batch the items instead.
Stop if the repeated queries come from a library you cannot change — cache or escalate to its owner.
Never fix N+1 by adding caching alone without fixing the query pattern.

title: Survive a third-party outage with a kill switch
mechanism_check: Confirm the dependency is the cause: your services are healthy, the vendor's status page or your traces say otherwise.
Determine what breaks without it: full outage, degraded feature, or cosmetic.
Check the contract: timeouts, retries, and circuit-breaker behavior already in place.
improvised_tools: A feature flag that disables the vendor call path as the kill switch.
Cached or default responses as the degraded-mode content.
The vendor status page plus your own synthetic check as the all-clear signal.
steps: Flip the kill switch to serve degraded mode and stop hammering the vendor.
Verify your error rate recovers and the degraded experience is acceptable.
Reduce retry storms first — backoff protects both you and the vendor.
Watch the vendor status and your synthetic check, not rumors, for recovery.
Re-enable gradually, then write the postmortem on why there was no switch sooner.
stop_conditions: Stop if degraded mode loses user data or money — stay down safely rather than corrupt.
Stop if the vendor outage is actually your misconfigured credentials — check auth before declaring their outage.
Never build new features on the vendor during their outage — stabilize first.

title: Restore a corrupted local database from backups and logs
mechanism_check: Confirm corruption versus app bug: do raw queries fail, or just the app.
Locate the newest intact backup and the write-ahead or transaction logs after it.
Decide the recovery point: the newest consistent state you can honestly defend.
improvised_tools: The backup file plus replayable logs as the reconstruction kit.
A scratch restore target so you never practice on the only copy.
Checksums or row counts as the integrity verdict.
steps: Stop all writers immediately and copy the corrupted files aside untouched.
Restore the newest backup to a scratch location, not over the original.
Replay logs forward to the newest consistent point, verifying checksums.
Spot-check critical tables by row count and recent known values.
Only then promote the restored copy and restart writers.
stop_conditions: Stop if there is no backup and no logs — say so plainly, do not fabricate data.
Stop if checksums fail after restore — the backup is bad, go one generation older.
Never restore over the corrupted original before verifying the restore works.

title: Build a health-check endpoint from scratch
mechanism_check: List what healthy means for this service: can it reach its database, its queue, its disk.
Decide depth: a shallow ping versus deep checks per dependency, with timeouts.
Know who calls it: load balancer, orchestrator, or humans — each wants a different shape.
improvised_tools: A single HTTP route as the check surface.
Per-dependency probes with short timeouts so one slow dependency does not hang the check.
Plain text or minimal JSON — no framework needed.
steps: Add a route that returns 200 and a version string with zero dependencies.
Add one probe per critical dependency, each with a one-second timeout.
Make any failed probe return 503 with the failing component named.
Wire the orchestrator or load balancer to the endpoint.
Test it by actually breaking a dependency and watching the status flip.
stop_conditions: Stop if the check itself needs the thing it checks — split shallow from deep.
Never let the health check do real work: no migrations, no heavy queries.
Never expose deep-check detail publicly — 200 or 503 only at the edge.

title: Migrate a schema with zero downtime, expand then contract
mechanism_check: Map every reader and writer of the changing tables, including background jobs and reports.
Confirm the deploy is multi-phase safe: old code and new code will briefly coexist.
Decide the contract window: how long both schema shapes must live side by side.
improvised_tools: The expand phase — additive-only changes — as the safe half.
Dual-write or backfill scripts as the bridge between shapes.
The contract phase — removing the old shape — scheduled only after all readers move.
steps: Expand: add the new column, table, or index without touching or removing the old.
Deploy code that writes to both shapes and reads from the old.
Backfill existing rows into the new shape in idempotent batches.
Switch readers to the new shape one consumer at a time, verifying each.
Contract: only after every reader is moved, drop the old shape in a later release.
stop_conditions: Stop if any writer cannot be dual-written — you do not have expand and contract, redesign.
Stop if the backfill cannot be idempotent — a half-run backfill must be safely re-runnable.
Never expand and contract in the same release — the safety is in the separation.

title: Backfill data safely with idempotent batches
mechanism_check: Define done precisely: which rows, what target value, how you will verify.
Confirm the write is idempotent: running it twice produces the same result as once.
Size the batch: small enough to not lock tables or spike replicas.
improvised_tools: Primary-key-ordered batches as the resumable unit of work.
A dry-run mode that logs what it would change.
A progress watermark — the last processed id — persisted outside the job.
steps: Write the backfill to process one batch by primary key range, then record the watermark.
Dry-run on a copy of production data and inspect a sample of changes.
Run against production in small batches with sleeps, watching replica lag.
If it dies, resume from the watermark — never from the start.
Verify with an independent count query, then delete the job code.
stop_conditions: Stop if replica lag crosses your threshold — slow down or pause, data safety beats speed.
Stop if the write is not idempotent — make it idempotent before running on production.
Never backfill without a dry run on production-shaped data.

title: Reproduce production data locally with anonymized fixtures
mechanism_check: Identify the minimum data the bug needs: which tables, which edge-case rows.
Classify the sensitivity: what must be anonymized or dropped before it leaves production.
Confirm policy allows the extraction — some data never leaves, no exceptions.
improvised_tools: A SQL dump filtered to the relevant slice, not the whole database.
An anonymization pass: fake names, emails, tokens, truncated secrets.
A seed script that rebuilds the fixture from scratch for teammates.
steps: Extract only the rows the bug touches, with a WHERE clause, not a full dump.
Anonymize every personal or secret field deterministically so relations survive.
Verify the fixture reproduces the bug locally before sharing it.
Commit the seed script, never the raw data, to the repo.
Delete the extracted files when the bug is fixed.
stop_conditions: Stop if policy forbids the data class entirely — build synthetic fixtures instead.
Stop if anonymization would destroy the bug's trigger — synthesize the edge case manually.
Never commit real production data, even just this once.

title: Combine two brittle scripts into one reliable job
mechanism_check: Read both scripts fully: what each does, what each assumes, where each fails silently.
Find the overlap: shared setup, shared credentials, duplicated logic.
Decide the single job's contract: inputs, outputs, exit codes, and what done means.
improvised_tools: One entrypoint script that calls the two as functions, not two cron lines.
Exit codes and strict error handling as the failure contract.
A log line per stage so the combined job stays debuggable.
steps: Extract each script's core into a function with explicit inputs and outputs.
Write the new entrypoint: setup once, run stage one, check, run stage two, check.
Make every failure loud: non-zero exit, a log line naming the stage, no silent skips.
Replace the two schedules with the one job and watch two full cycles.
Delete the old scripts only after the new job proves itself.
stop_conditions: Stop if the scripts have conflicting dependencies — isolate before combining.
Stop if either script's failure mode is silently wrong output — fix that first, combining hides it.
Never combine by copy-pasting both bodies into one file — extract, then compose.

title: Write the runbook you wish the last incident had
mechanism_check: Pick the last real incident: what did responders grope for in the first ten minutes.
List the questions asked on the call: where are the logs, who owns this, how do we roll back.
Separate timeless procedure from incident-specific detail.
improvised_tools: The incident timeline as the raw material — real confusion, real fixes.
Checklists, not prose: responders read bullets under pressure.
One owner per runbook, with a review date.
steps: Write the symptom-to-diagnosis section first: what to check in the first five minutes.
Add the exact commands: rollback, flag flips, log queries — copy-paste ready.
Name the owners and escalation paths, with no dead links.
Have someone who was not in the incident follow it cold and fix what confuses them.
Schedule a review every quarter — runbooks rot.
stop_conditions: Stop if the runbook needs more than one page for the critical path — split it.
Never write a runbook from imagination — ground every line in a real incident.
If the cold reader cannot complete it, it is not done.

title: Read unfamiliar code with intent
mechanism_check: State your question before opening the code: what decision are you trying to make.
Find the entry points: main, handlers, or the module the bug report names.
Identify the code's age and churn: new code reads differently from ten-year-old survivors.
improvised_tools: The test suite as the executable specification of intent.
Git blame and history as the archaeology of why.
A scratch diagram of the call flow, drawn by hand.
steps: Read the tests first to learn what the code promises.
Trace one real request or call from entry to exit, ignoring branches.
Note the invariants: what must be true at each boundary.
Read the history of the strangest line — there is usually a scar.
Write a three-sentence summary: what it does, what it assumes, what would break it.
stop_conditions: Stop reading when you can answer your original question — depth beyond that is procrastination.
Stop if there are no tests and no history — say the code is unreadable and budget accordingly.
Never refactor code you have not yet understood — reading is the prerequisite.

title: Write the commit message your future self needs
mechanism_check: Know the audience: a future debugger at 2am, not your present teammates.
Separate what — the diff shows it — from why, which only you know.
Check the project's convention: conventional commits, ticket links, or freeform.
improvised_tools: The ticket or bug report as the why-source.
The diff itself as the what — never restate it.
A template: context, decision, consequence.
steps: Write the first line as an imperative summary under seventy-two characters.
Add the context: what was broken or requested, in one or two lines.
Record the why: the alternatives considered and why this one won.
Note consequences: migrations, flag removals, follow-ups.
Read it back pretending you know nothing — if it confuses you now, it will later.
stop_conditions: Stop if the message needs a paragraph to explain the diff — the change is too big, split it.
Never write fix-bug or wip on a shared branch.
Never rewrite shared history to fix a message — add a follow-up note instead.

title: Keep a failure journal to build debugging intuition
mechanism_check: Notice your own pattern: do you always suspect the network, the cache, the last deploy.
Pick a capture moment: right after the fix, while the surprise is fresh.
Keep it private and honest — this is training data, not a report.
improvised_tools: A plain text file or notebook as the journal — no tooling needed.
Four fields per entry: symptom, first theory, actual cause, lesson.
A monthly re-read as the compounding step.
steps: After each bug, write the symptom in one line.
Write what you suspected first, before you knew the answer.
Write the actual cause and where the evidence pointed.
Extract one lesson: a check to run earlier next time.
Re-read monthly and watch your first theories get faster.
stop_conditions: Stop if entries become blame narratives — the journal is about mechanisms, not people.
Stop logging bugs you did not personally debug — secondhand entries teach nothing.
If you stop re-reading, the journal is write-only — shrink it to the four fields until it sticks.

title: Design the API contract before writing code
mechanism_check: List the consumers first: who calls this, and what do they actually need.
Decide the stability promise: what can change without breaking callers.
Identify the failure shapes: what errors look like, not just the happy path.
improvised_tools: A written contract: endpoints, shapes, and error codes in plain text.
Example requests and responses as the executable spec.
A consumer review — the caller reads it before you build.
steps: Draft the resources and operations in plain language, no code.
Write three example calls: happy path, validation error, and not-found.
Get the consumer to sign off on the examples — this is the handshake.
Only then implement, with the examples as your first tests.
Version from day one, even if the version is just v1 draft.
stop_conditions: Stop if consumers cannot agree on the shape — the domain is not understood yet, spike first.
Never let implementation details leak into the contract — no database ids as public ids.
If the contract needs more than a page, split the API.

title: Turn a spike into a written decision record
mechanism_check: Confirm the spike answered its question: time-boxed and question-first, or it was tinkering.
Extract the decision: what was chosen, and what was rejected.
Identify who needs to know: future maintainers and adjacent teams.
improvised_tools: A short decision record: context, options, decision, consequences.
The spike code as the evidence appendix, not the deliverable.
A shared location where records actually get read.
steps: Write the context: what question the spike was answering and why it mattered.
List the options tried, with one-line verdicts each.
State the decision and the reasons that carried it.
Record consequences: what this choice forecloses or commits to.
File it where the team looks, and link it from the code it governs.
stop_conditions: Stop if the spike answered nothing — say so and do not dress it up.
Never ship spike code as production code — spikes are for learning.
If the decision is reversible and cheap, skip the record — document the irreversible ones.

title: Give a code review that teaches
mechanism_check: Read the change's intent first: the description and tests before the diff.
Separate blocking issues from suggestions from nits — they are different speech acts.
Check your own state: tired reviewers write cruel reviews.
improvised_tools: Questions instead of verdicts: ask what happens when X rather than declaring it wrong.
The codebase's own conventions as the neutral authority.
Praise for the specific good choice, not generic cheer.
steps: Start by stating what you think the change does — let the author correct you.
Flag correctness and security issues as blocking, with the failing case spelled out.
Offer suggestions as options with reasoning, not commands.
Batch nits or let the linter own them — never lead with style.
Approve promptly when it is good enough — reviews are not redesign sessions.
stop_conditions: Stop if you are rewriting the author's approach entirely — take it to a design conversation instead.
Stop reviewing when you are skimming — say so and hand it to someone fresh.
Never approve code you did not read.

title: Learn a new stack in two weeks
mechanism_check: Define learned: what you must be able to build or fix by day fourteen.
Map what transfers: your existing mental models are the scaffolding.
Find the stack's own idioms — every stack punishes tourists.
improvised_tools: The official tutorial plus one real project, not ten tutorials.
The stack's error messages as the curriculum — break things deliberately.
A practitioner to ask the three questions tutorials never answer.
steps: Days one to three: build the canonical tutorial app and deploy it somewhere real.
Days four to seven: rebuild one small thing you already know, in the new stack.
Days eight to ten: deliberately break it — errors teach the runtime model.
Days eleven to fourteen: ship one tiny production thing or a faithful prototype.
Write down the stack's three biggest surprises — what the docs never said.
stop_conditions: Stop tutorial-hopping after the first one — building beats watching.
Stop if two weeks becomes two months of prep — scope the goal down, not the timeline out.
Never claim fluency at day fourteen — claim the ability to build and debug, honestly.

title: Write documentation people actually read
mechanism_check: Know the reader's job: what are they trying to do when they open this.
Find where docs fail today: the questions asked repeatedly are the missing pages.
Decide the doc's half-life: tutorial, how-to, or reference — each rots differently.
improvised_tools: Real user questions as the table of contents.
Copy-pasteable examples as the core content.
A last-verified date as the honesty label.
steps: Write the title as the reader's question, not the feature's name.
Open with the working example, then explain — never the reverse.
Keep each page to one task; link, do not sprawl.
Test every command by running it fresh before publishing.
Date-stamp it and assign an owner for the next verification.
stop_conditions: Stop if the doc describes aspirational behavior — document what ships.
Stop writing when the page exceeds one task — split it.
Never document a workaround without linking the ticket that will kill it.

title: Estimate work honestly with ranges and confidence
mechanism_check: Separate the known from the unknown: what is specified versus what is fog.
Check your own history: do you chronically halve or double.
Identify the riskiest unknown — it owns the estimate.
improvised_tools: Ranges, not points: three to five days instead of a single four-day guess.
Explicit confidence: what would have to be true for the low end.
The spike as the fog-clearing tool for the biggest unknown.
steps: Break the work until no piece is bigger than a day or two.
Estimate each piece as a range, naming the assumption behind each.
Add the risks as line items, not padding hidden in the numbers.
State confidence plainly: what could still surprise you.
Track actuals against estimates and calibrate quarterly.
stop_conditions: Stop if you are pressured to a single number — give the range and name the risk.
Never estimate someone else's unfamiliar work without their input.
If the range spans more than three times, spike first — the fog is the estimate.

title: Mentor a junior through their first real bug
mechanism_check: Assess where they actually are: can they reproduce it, or are they still reading.
Resist the rescue urge: your job is their growth, not the fix speed.
Identify the one skill this bug can teach: bisection, reading traces, or asking for help.
improvised_tools: Questions as the primary tool: ask what they know so far before offering any hint.
The repro from entry developer-002 as the shared ground.
A visible timer — struggle has a budget, then you pair.
steps: Have them state the bug and their current theory out loud.
Ask what evidence would confirm or kill the theory, then let them gather it.
Give hints as smaller questions, never as answers.
If they stall past the agreed budget, switch to pairing (entry developer-040) without shame.
Debrief: what will they check first next time.
stop_conditions: Stop if you catch yourself typing the fix — hands off the keyboard.
Stop if frustration replaces curiosity — name it, take a break.
Never measure mentoring by fix speed — measure by what they can do alone next month.

title: Refactor with the strangler approach, never the big bang
mechanism_check: Map the module's boundaries: what calls in, what it calls out.
Confirm the strangler is possible: can new code coexist beside old behind a seam.
Identify the seam: the narrowest interface you can intercept.
improvised_tools: The seam — interface, facade, or flag — as the strangling point.
Characterization tests that pin current behavior before you touch anything.
Small, shippable slices — each one leaves the system working.
steps: Write characterization tests capturing the old behavior, quirks included.
Build the seam so new and old implementations can coexist.
Migrate one slice at a time behind the seam, tests green throughout.
Delete the old slice only when nothing routes to it anymore.
Repeat until the old module is an empty shell, then remove it.
stop_conditions: Stop if you cannot write the characterization tests — you do not understand it well enough to strangle.
Stop if a slice cannot ship independently — the seam is in the wrong place.
Never run old and new side by side in production without a way to compare their outputs.

title: Combine two design patterns into one working solution
mechanism_check: Name the actual problem first: patterns serve problems, not resumes.
Verify each pattern fits a real force in the problem — not decoration.
Check the combination does not fight itself: what each pattern assumes.
improvised_tools: The problem statement as the referee between patterns.
A spike (entry developer-025) to test the combination cheaply.
The codebase's existing patterns as the consistency check.
steps: Write the problem and its forces in plain language.
Pick the first pattern for the dominant force, the second for the secondary.
Spike the combination against a real scenario from the codebase.
Name the hybrid honestly in the decision record — future readers need the map.
Implement with the patterns' boundaries visible, not blended into mush.
stop_conditions: Stop if you cannot name the forces each pattern addresses — it is decoration.
Stop if the combination needs a paragraph to explain — simplify to one pattern.
Never combine patterns to look clever — clever is a maintenance cost.

title: Set up a code-review culture on a team of three
mechanism_check: Name the real resistance: speed, ego, or nobody knowing what a good review looks like.
Check the current state honestly: rubber stamps, bottlenecks, or no reviews at all.
Decide what culture means here: every change reviewed, feedback kind, merges unblocked.
improvised_tools: A short written norm: what reviewers owe and what authors owe.
Small pull requests as the cultural unit — big diffs kill review culture.
A rotating reviewer so knowledge spreads instead of siloing.
steps: Agree on the norm together: review within a day, blocking versus advisory labels.
Shrink changes: if it does not fit a review, it does not fit a merge.
Rotate reviewers so everyone reads everyone else's code.
Model the tone from the top: questions, specifics, and prompt approvals.
Review the norm itself monthly — culture is maintained, not installed.
stop_conditions: Stop if reviews consistently take days — the batch size is the problem, not the people.
Stop if feedback turns personal — pause and reset the norm before continuing.
Never let one person become the mandatory reviewer — that is a bottleneck with a title.

title: Triage a bug backlog as a team in one hour
mechanism_check: Count the backlog honestly: how many, how old, how many are already fixed or obsolete.
Agree on the triage outputs: priority, owner, or closed — every bug leaves with one.
Time-box ruthlessly: one hour, no deep dives.
improvised_tools: A shared screen and a timer as the forcing functions.
Three buckets — now, later, never — plus needs-repro.
The reporter or area owner as the tiebreaker on priority.
steps: Sort oldest first — age is information.
For each bug: reproduce in sixty seconds or mark needs-repro and move on.
Assign each bug a bucket — now, later, or never — with an owner for now.
Close duplicates and already-fixed bugs on the spot — celebrate the deletions.
Publish the resulting priority list where the team works.
stop_conditions: Stop debating any single bug past two minutes — mark it needs-owner and move on.
Stop if the backlog grows faster than triage clears it — the intake is the problem.
Never triage alone and present verdicts — the team must own the priorities.

title: Hand off on-call cleanly between humans
mechanism_check: List what the incoming person must know: active incidents, known flaky systems, pending changes.
Check the outgoing person's state: tired humans hand off badly.
Confirm the mechanics: paging actually routes to the new person.
improvised_tools: A written handoff note: active issues, watch items, recent changes.
A live overlap call for anything non-trivial.
A test page to prove the routing works.
steps: Outgoing writes the handoff note before the call, not during.
Walk through active incidents and what good looks like for each.
Name the systems most likely to page and their first-response moves.
Transfer the pager and send a test page to confirm.
Incoming acknowledges in writing — the handoff is not done until then.
stop_conditions: Stop if the outgoing person cannot summarize the state — the on-call load was already unsafe.
Never hand off mid-incident without the incoming joining the incident call.
If pages fire during handoff, the outgoing stays until it is stable.

title: Run incident command with a voice call and a shared doc
mechanism_check: Confirm someone is actually in charge: incidents without a commander get parallel chaos.
Separate the roles: commander decides, scribe records, responders work.
Check the comms: one call, one doc — not five side channels.
improvised_tools: The incident commander role as the single decision point.
A shared timeline doc as the collective memory.
A voice call as the fast channel, text as the record.
steps: Declare the incident and name the commander in the first minute.
Commander states the current theory and assigns the next two actions — nothing more.
Scribe timestamps every action and finding in the shared doc.
Reassess every fifteen minutes: are we closer, or is it time to escalate.
Declare resolution explicitly and freeze the timeline for the postmortem.
stop_conditions: Stop debugging and escalate if two reassessments show no progress.
Stop if the commander starts doing the technical work — commanders coordinate.
Never run an incident over chat alone — voice for speed, doc for truth.

title: Coordinate a deploy freeze during an incident
mechanism_check: Confirm the incident is real and active — freezes cost momentum, spend it wisely.
Identify what freeze covers: all deploys, or all but the fix.
Find who can declare and lift it: the authority must be named before the incident.
improvised_tools: A single announcement channel as the source of truth.
The freeze declared with a scope and an expiry, not open-ended.
An exception process for the fix itself — the thing that ends the incident.
steps: Commander declares the freeze: scope, reason, and who can grant exceptions.
Announce in the one channel everyone watches — no side-channel freezes.
Park in-flight deploys explicitly: each owner confirms their state.
Allow only the incident fix through, with commander approval.
Lift the freeze publicly with a summary — silence breeds shadow deploys.
stop_conditions: Stop extending the freeze past the incident plus one review cycle — stale freezes get ignored.
Never freeze without naming who lifts it.
If teams start deploying around the freeze, the process failed — fix the trust, not the rule.

title: Escalate without panic using a written ladder
mechanism_check: Define the rungs before the incident: responder, incident commander, engineering lead, executive.
Set the triggers: what conditions move you up a rung — time, blast radius, or stuckness.
Confirm contact paths actually work: stale escalation lists are fiction.
improvised_tools: The written ladder as the panic substitute — follow the rungs.
Pre-agreed triggers so escalation is a decision, not an emotion.
A template message: situation, impact, what you need, what you have tried.
steps: When a trigger hits, escalate immediately — delay is the failure mode.
Send the template: situation, impact, need, attempts so far.
The higher rung takes command or explicitly delegates back — no ambiguity.
Each rung brings resources, not blame: access, authority, or extra hands.
Afterward, check whether the triggers fired at the right time and adjust.
stop_conditions: Stop if escalation becomes the first move for every alert — the triggers are too loose.
Never skip rungs to reach an executive — the ladder exists to protect focus.
If the top rung is unreachable during a real incident, that is the postmortem's first finding.

title: Run a blameless postmortem that actually fixes things
mechanism_check: Wait for calm: postmortems need distance, ideally within a week.
Gather the timeline from the incident doc — memory lies, timestamps do not.
Confirm blamelessness is real: if people fear it, they will not speak.
improvised_tools: The timeline walk as the structure — what happened, in order.
Action items with owners and dates as the output.
A facilitator who was not in the hot seat.
steps: Walk the timeline together: what happened, when, what was tried.
Ask why at each surprise — five times or until the system, not the person, answers.
Write action items that change the system: alerts, runbooks, automation — not be more careful.
Assign every item an owner and a date, and track them like features.
Share the writeup with the wider team — incidents are tuition.
stop_conditions: Stop if the room starts naming culprits — reset to blameless or end the session.
Never file a postmortem with zero action items — something always can improve.
If action items die untracked, the postmortem was theater — track them publicly.

title: Pair program to unstick a teammate in an hour
mechanism_check: Confirm they are actually stuck: thirty-plus minutes with no new evidence, not just thinking.
Agree on the goal: unstuck and learning, not you driving.
Check energy: pairing while frustrated needs a reset first.
improvised_tools: The one-hour box as the container — pairing without end becomes dependence.
Driver-navigator rotation as the structure.
Their machine, their code — you are the guest.
steps: Have them narrate the current state: theory, evidence, what they have tried.
Take navigator first: ask questions, suggest the next experiment, do not touch the keyboard.
Rotate to driver only to demonstrate a technique, then hand back.
When the unblock lands, have them explain it back in their own words.
End with the one check they will run first next time.
stop_conditions: Stop if you are doing all the thinking — slow down to their pace or stop the session.
Stop if the hour ends without progress — the problem needs a different approach, not more pairing.
Never pair as surveillance — it is offered help, not assigned oversight.

title: Onboard a new developer in a week with no onboarding docs
mechanism_check: Audit what actually exists: a README, a working setup script, or nothing but lore.
Identify the buddy: one human who answers questions within the hour.
Define week-one done: environment running, one small change shipped, one teammate known.
improvised_tools: The buddy as the living documentation.
A setup checklist built live as the newcomer hits each snag.
Their fresh-eyes questions as the raw material for the docs you will write.
steps: Day one: get the environment running together — fix the setup script as you go.
Days two to three: assign a tiny, real, shippable task with the buddy nearby.
Day four: have them write down every snag — that becomes the onboarding doc.
Day five: they demo what they shipped and what confused them.
Commit the resulting onboarding doc — the next hire inherits it.
stop_conditions: Stop if setup takes more than two days — the environment is the bug, fix it first.
Never assign critical-path work in week one.
If the newcomer stops asking questions, check in — silence is stuckness.

title: Hold a design review that converges
mechanism_check: Confirm the design is reviewable: written down, with the problem and options stated.
Invite the right room: stakeholders and one skeptic, not the whole company.
Set the decision: who decides, and by when — reviews without deciders do not converge.
improvised_tools: The written proposal as the anchor — no slideware ambushes.
Time-boxed discussion per section as the convergence engine.
A decision log capturing what was decided and what was deferred.
steps: Author presents the problem and options in ten minutes, no more.
Reviewers ask clarifying questions first — critique comes second.
Debate the tradeoffs against the stated requirements, not tastes.
The decider calls it: approved, approved with changes, or rejected with reasons.
Log the decision and revisit only on new information.
stop_conditions: Stop if the review becomes a redesign workshop — send it back for a revision.
Stop if key stakeholders are missing — reschedule, do not decide without them.
Never let a review end without a recorded decision.

title: Split on-call load fairly to prevent burnout
mechanism_check: Measure the actual load: pages per rotation, night pages, incident hours — not feelings.
Find the unfairness: who gets the worst weeks, who never does.
Check the human cost: who is tired, who is quiet about it.
improvised_tools: Rotation data as the fairness evidence.
Explicit compensation: time off after bad weeks, not just thanks.
A secondary on-call so the primary is never truly alone.
steps: Publish the load data: pages, nights, and incident hours per person.
Design the rotation so nights and holidays spread evenly — write the rule down.
Add a secondary who shadows and can take over.
Grant recovery time after brutal rotations, automatically.
Review the data quarterly and rebalance — fairness drifts.
stop_conditions: Stop if the same person keeps volunteering for everything — heroics are a burnout signal.
Never punish someone for escalating — the ladder exists to be used.
If the load is unfair because the team is too small, say so — the fix is hiring, not heroism.

title: Run a game day to practice failing on purpose
mechanism_check: Pick a realistic failure: the one the team fears most, scoped to be survivable.
Confirm the blast radius is contained: staging, or production with guardrails and an abort plan.
Get explicit permission: game days without buy-in are just outages.
improvised_tools: The failure scenario as the script.
The incident roles from entry developer-036, practiced for real.
Observers who take notes while the responders work.
steps: Write the scenario: what breaks, what the team should notice, what good response looks like.
Brief the responders on the rules and the abort conditions.
Inject the failure and run it like a real incident — commander, scribe, timeline.
Debrief immediately: what was slow, what was missing, what surprised everyone.
Turn every gap into a tracked action item.
stop_conditions: Abort the moment real user impact escapes the planned scope — no exceptions.
Stop if the team treats it as a joke — reschedule with seriousness.
Never run a game day without the abort plan tested first.
